summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for mental health support despite lacking mechanisms to safely govern evolving risk. Existing safety approaches primarily detect risk but rarely shape how models respond as conversational risk unfolds. We developed a portable, model-external safety governance architecture that combines contextual risk detection, reasoning-based verification, and protocol-guided response generation for multi-turn mental health interactions. Using synthetic conversations grounded in real-world mental health narratives, the architecture’s performance was assessed with GPT-5-chat and Qwen3.5-27B, increasing clinician-preferred escalation responses by 25.6–59.2 pp, while achieving high risk detection performance (specificity: 0.85 (95%CI: 0.78;0.91), sensitivity: 0.92 (95%CI: 0.89;0.95)). Performance remained stable across conversation length and across models (proprietary and open-source), with preliminary evidence showing that rapport and connection were preserved. These findings demonstrate that clinically-grounded governance can extend beyond risk detection to improve how LLMs manage evolving mental health risk, providing a framework for scalable safety governance.
